subject: A tilt-shift miniature: the spectrum built as a row of thin fins on a model base, with an upright glass plane of focus standing across it that captures the fins inside its depth of field as solid and leaves the rest hollow and doubled.
controls: focus: position. The plane of focus and its two depth-of-field lines on the base slide along the row, 100 Hz to 8 kHz, about 260 px of screen travel; fins entering it turn solid, fins leaving it go hollow.
tilt: shape. The base tips: fin heights ramp along the row about the plane of focus, so at −6 the near end towers and the far end sinks to stubs, at +6 the reverse (each fin 8–56 px).
blur: position. Each fin outside the depth of field casts a hollow ghost of itself set back into the base; blur pushes the ghost from 0 to ~14 px back, further for fins further from focus.
mix: position. No twin in the optics; a plain scale along the base's front edge (octave ticks, a 1.5 px bar) fills from 0 to the full length.
reference: library/meikyu-capture/README.md (P13: the machine's rule drawn as a physical thing) beside library/toro-blocks/contact.png (hidden-line boxes)
stretch: Why this machine might be the exception: P13 asks for the machine's own rule drawn as a physical thing with the same shape, and tilt's rule is literally an optical one (a plane of focus that keeps a band sharp and lets the rest go soft). The capture is the depth of field: what's inside it is sharp. Where it doesn't fit: P13 is a player/function pattern built on items being let through to play; here nothing is let through, only sharpened, and two of the four controls (tilt, mix) have no twin in the optics, so half the screen is scenery.
risks: Honest verdict on the stretch: it fits for focus and blur, and doesn't for tilt (a sloped base is a stand-in) or mix (a ruler in the corner, which P13 itself warns looks bolted on).
Twenty-two fins in a row read as a bookshelf or dominoes before they read as a spectrum; the glass plane is the only cue that this is about focus.
The camera is dimetric (24°/30°), not true isometric, to fit 300 px of row into a 200 px body; a strict 30° row would need ~170 px of drop.
Close to toro's hidden-line block field in look; the composition (one row, one plane) has to keep it from reading as a copy.
